note: Source says Want of zeal or daring was certainly not the fault; candidate drops certainly.
replacement: After this address Nicias at once led the army forward. The Syracusans were not expecting an immediate engagement at that moment, and some had even gone away to the town, which was close by. These now ran up as hard as they could and, though late, took their places here and there in the main body as fast as they joined it. Certainly, neither in this battle nor in the others was the fault of the Syracusans a want of zeal or daring. They were not inferior in courage, so far as their military science could carry them, but when that failed them they were forced to give up their resolution also. On this occasion they had not supposed that the Athenians would begin the attack, and they were forced to stand on their defense at short notice. Even so, they at once took up their arms and advanced to meet them. First the stone-throwers, slingers and archers of both armies began skirmishing, and routed or were routed by one another, as might be expected between light troops. Next, soothsayers brought forward the usual victims, and trumpeters urged on the heavy infantry to the charge. So they advanced. The Syracusans fought for their country, and each individual for his safety that day and his liberty hereafter. In the enemy’s army, the Athenians fought to make another’s country theirs and to save their own from suffering by their defeat. The Argives and the independent allies fought to help them get what they had come for, and to earn by victory another sight of the country they had left behind. The subject allies owed most of their ardor to the desire for self-preservation, which they could hope for only if victorious. Next to this, as a secondary motive, came the chance of serving on easier terms after helping the Athenians to a fresh conquest.

note: Purpose clause (might either have to leave or be less able) became a flat prediction with added at least.
replacement: The Syracusans heard him out and voted everything as he advised. They elected three generals: Hermocrates himself, Heraclides, son of Lysimachus, and Sicanus, son of Execestes. They also sent envoys to Corinth and Lacedaemon to obtain a force of allies to join them. The envoys were to persuade the Lacedaemonians to take up the war against the Athenians openly and in real earnest, for the Syracusans’ sake, so that the Athenians might either have to leave Sicily or be less able to send reinforcements to their army there.
